newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA FOREX POLICY KEEPS MARKETS ON TENTERHOOKS.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA FOREX POLICY KEEPS MARKETS ON TENTERHOOKS.

text.p: Mixed signals from officials on how and when exchange controls will be lifted have left South African markets confused and the rand vulnerable, analysts and foreign exchange dealers said on Wednesday.
Comments from Finance Minister Trevor Manuel, Finance Director General Maria Ramos and Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals on the central issue dominating investor sentiment have baffled players.

On Tuesday, Manuel said he had no deadline for scrapping controls, was not talking to the IMF about a loan and, for the first time, raised the prospect of continuing some controls in the form of a prudential requirement on savings, limiting pension fund investments overseas.
On Wednesday, Ramos reiterated the possibility of a prudential requirement on institutions and reaffirmed that government policy was for a phased lifting of controls.
But in a front page interview with Business Day, Stals laid out conditions for a one-off -- or "big bang" -- approach to abolishing resstrictions on the convertibility of the rand.

Stals said necessary measures could include taking a $2 billion standy facility from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to help boost reserves, plus an economic "restructuring" package over and above last June's macro-economic strategy.

"Stals seems to be hinting that a big bang might be the way forward yet Manuel is saying we still have to decide. Some clear commitment is certainly necessary," said ABN AMRO economist Anastasia Gekis.

Other analysts agreed the blurred policy message was adding to uncertainty and fuelling pressure on the rand which hit a record low of 4.77 against the U.S. dollar last week. It has since recovered to around 4.70.

"The whole process of exchange control relaxation and currency depreciation needs to be managed. At the moment there seems to be no management," said Mike Brown, economist at stockbroker Frankel Pollak.
However, Brown said the Reserve Bank appeared to be busy with ideas which could be put to government soon.

"There is a lot of work being done at the Reserve Bank, a lot of midnight oil being burnt. I would say we are going to have some sort of monetary or currency stabilisation package announced in the next month or so."
This could include a specific timetable for easing remaining controls, aiming first at individuals who might, for example, be allowed to open dollar accounts with South Africa banks.
There might also be a hike in interest rates -- already discounted by money markets -- which could help attract inflows.
Economists argue abolition of controls on residents is vital, both to allow the market to determine to true value of the rand and to signal government confidence in the economy.
But Stals and Manuel have made clear no further relaxation can be allowed while reserves remain precariously low, at around four weeks import cover.

An IMF loan, which Stals is thought to favour, would be one way to bridge the trough in reserves which BOE NatWest economist Nick Barnardt expects to improve sharply as the current account moves back into surplus from mid-1997.

IMF managing director Michel Camdessus has said that the IMF facility -- which would more than double foreign reserves -- could be used to bolster the capital account during a phase of liberalisation.
But some members of the ruling African National Congress are wary of the stigma attached to IMF aid, following unpopular IMF interventions elsewhere in Africa.
Barnardt sees in Stals' latest comments a possibility of major steps to liberalise the rand sometime in 1997, although nothing is likely to be implemented before the March 12 budget.
But the uncertainty continues. "It is an interesting word game to watch," he said.
